Trump requested several amendments to the agreement that his envoys reached with their Iranian counterparts during a Situation room meeting on Friday, according to a senior administration official and a second source briefed on the matter.

Trump wants the deal and expects to finalize it soon, but wants to reinforce several points that are important to him — especially around Iranian nuclear materials, two U.S. officials said. 

Trump's request launched a new round of back-and-forth between the parties that could last several days.

Trump announced Friday that he would convene the situation room meeting on the deal, and seemed to suggest that he was inclined to accept.

A White House official told reporters after the meeting that Trump "will only make a deal that is good for America, satisfies its red lines and ensures that Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon."

A high ranking Ianian official, a member of the negotiations team, told the state media Tasnim that it is “a bare-faced effrontery” (استکبار بدون مرز) ; although two US officials claimed earlier in the week that Tehran was ready to sign and that it was all up to Trump.

According to the two sources, Trump has asked his team to make changes to the draft clauses concerning the Iranian nuclear program.

In its current form, the MOU includes a commitment by Iran not to seek nuclear weapons, but no specific concessions beyond that.

He says there will be a 60-day window to negotiate Iran's nuclear commitments and U.S. sanctions relief, with the first issues on the agenda being how to dispose of Iran's stockpile of enriched uranium and limit further enrichment.

“It's more specific about how the United States gets the material and the timing,” a senior administration official said, referring to enriched uranium.

Another source said that Trump also wants to change part of the wording regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

The US official said that Trump had learned that it would be about three days before the Iranians would return with an answer. “They are literally in caves and they are not using e-mail,” the senior administration official said.

Europe’s Next Winter: Expensive, Dry, and Self‑Inflicted

European traders are already pricing in another brutal season. Winter power contracts for late 2026–early 2027 are trading more than 20 percent above next year’s benchmark, the highest winter premium since the 2022 energy crisis. 

The signal is clear: markets expect tight supply and painful prices for households and industry.

The reasons are layered and ugly. Gas storage is lower than at this point before last winter, when Europe was still scrambling for alternatives to Russian pipeline gas. 
At the same time, hydropower reservoirs are depleted after dry seasons in key regions like the Nordics, cutting into what used to be the continent’s “cheap battery.” 

In countries like Germany and Italy, winter quarter contracts are rising faster than full‑year prices, a classic sign of fear about cold‑weather shortages.

Officially, Brussels calls this a “transition.” In practice, the EU has voted to phase out Russian LNG by the end of 2026 and pipeline gas by 2027, banned new Russian gas contracts and ordered existing ones wound down, while betting on global LNG, renewables and demand reduction to fill the gap. 

When everything works — mild weather, full storage, no shocks in the Strait of Hormuz — the system just about holds. When water is low, gas is tight and new crises erupt, the price of virtue shows up directly in utility bills and factory closures.

The result is a slow‑burn de‑industrialization risk that even Brussels now admits in footnotes. 

High and volatile energy prices, layered with green regulation and tighter emissions rules, are making whole sectors — chemicals, metals, paper, fertilizer — borderline unviable in Europe while the U.S., the Gulf and parts of Asia woo them with cheaper energy and subsidies. 

Politicians sell this as climate leadership; for many European workers it feels more like being told to sacrifice their jobs so that their leaders can brag at conferences.

None of this changes the physics: the continent needs huge amounts of stable electricity and heat, and right now it’s entering winter with less cheap hydro, more expensive gas, and no real replacement for the Russian flows it chose to cut off. 

The crisis wasn’t a one‑off spike in 2022 — it’s a new normal. Europe insisted it could fight Russia, decarbonize fast and keep energy affordable all at once. The coming winter looks like another reminder that, in the real world, you don’t get all three.

Trump’s Iran “Final Determination”: War, Peace, or Just Optics

Trump has managed to turn a Middle East ceasefire into a personal cliffhanger. 

He’s spent weeks zigzagging between bragging about a “great and meaningful” deal with Iran and threatening to restart strikes, and now promises a “final determination” from the Situation Room that somehow never materializes. 

The region is stuck watching his mood swings, not a strategy.

The draft deal on the table is brutally simple: the U.S. and Israel stop bombing Iran; Iran fully reopens the Strait of Hormuz and lets oil and gas flow again. 

Everything hard — the nuclear program, sanctions, regional militias — gets kicked to “later rounds” that may or may not exist. 

Trump tells his base this is total victory and demands that Iran let the U.S. “remove and destroy” enriched uranium stockpiles. Iranian officials tell their public they’ve survived regime‑change plans and conceded almost nothing on the core of their nuclear posture. 

Both cannot be true in the long run, but both can be true long enough to survive the next news cycle.

Inside Iran, nobody is fooled. Ordinary Iranians who dared hope war might finally break the regime’s grip now see the likely outcome: the Islamic Republic trades a partial reopening of the economy and safety for its leadership in exchange for tactical concessions, while the population gets more repression plus inflation plus the same ruling elite. 

As one engineer says in the piece, any deal “would mostly serve to guarantee the survival of the Islamic Republic.” The war that was sold from Washington as a blow against tyranny becomes, in Tehran, another reason for the state to tighten the screws and claim victory for “resistance.”

In Washington, the script is just as cynical. Hawks scream that even this thin framework is a “catastrophe,” because it doesn’t dismantle Iran’s entire missile and nuclear program on camera. 

Trump’s team insists he’s “patient” and that U.S. stockpiles can easily handle another round of fighting, despite months of leaks about depleted munitions. 

The war is deeply unpopular at home, gas prices are painful, and yet the administration wants to be seen neither as retreating nor as stuck in a forever war. 

The answer is a half‑deal: enough to calm oil markets, vague enough to keep all options open.

Israel and Iran’s hard‑liners are, perversely, aligned on one point: they both suspect this agreement could limit their ability to keep hitting each other in the gray zone. 

Netanyahu publicly talks about “deepening operations” against Hezbollah in Lebanon and insists Israel will always retain the right to act, deal or no deal. Iranian hawks call Trump’s demands “excessive” and warn against trusting Washington at all. 

Each needs the other as a permanent enemy, not as a party to a stable framework. That’s why every “historic” agreement in this region is written with invisible ink.

Three months after launching a war he framed as the beginning of the end for the Islamic Republic, Trump is now negotiating a document that leaves its leadership intact, its nuclear file largely deferred, and its claim to have survived U.S.–Israeli pressure stronger than before. 

Tehran gets to say it stood up to America; Trump gets to say he forced Iran to the table; Israel gets to keep its “right to defend itself” against everyone, everywhere. 

The only people who don’t get anything out of this “final determination” are the ones who have been under the bombs — and they’re not in the room.
